title: Sleep & Your Weight
summary: Poor sleep disrupts the hormones that control hunger and fullness - making it harder to eat well even when you intend to. The connection between sleep and weight is better established than most people realise.

steps.heading: The sleep–weight connection
steps.body: Multiple large studies have found that people who consistently sleep fewer than 7 hours per night have higher rates of obesity and weight gain over time. This is not just about having more waking hours to eat - the mechanisms go deeper. Sleep deprivation directly changes the hormones that govern how hungry you feel and how quickly you feel full.

steps.heading: Ghrelin: the hunger hormone
steps.body: Ghrelin is a hormone produced mainly in the stomach that signals hunger to your brain. When you are sleep-deprived, ghrelin levels rise - meaning your body sends stronger hunger signals than it would after a full night's sleep. Studies have found that a single night of insufficient sleep can increase ghrelin and reported hunger levels the following day, particularly cravings for calorie-dense foods.

steps.heading: Leptin: the fullness hormone
steps.body: Leptin is produced by fat cells and signals to the brain that you have had enough to eat. Poor sleep suppresses leptin levels, meaning your brain receives a weaker "I'm full" signal even after eating. The combination of elevated ghrelin and reduced leptin after sleep deprivation creates a hormonal environment that makes overeating significantly easier and more likely.

steps.heading: What you tend to crave when tired
steps.body: Sleep deprivation does not just increase overall appetite - it specifically increases cravings for high-calorie, sweet, and salty foods. Research suggests this happens partly because the reward and decision-making regions of the brain are more reactive to food cues when you are tired, and the prefrontal cortex - responsible for impulse control - is less able to override those impulses. Willpower is genuinely harder to access on poor sleep.

steps.heading: Sleep and physical activity
steps.body: Fatigue from poor sleep reduces motivation to exercise and decreases physical performance when you do. Over time, a pattern of poor sleep can reduce both the amount and intensity of physical activity, contributing further to a calorie surplus. Recovery from exercise also requires adequate sleep - muscles repair and adapt during deep sleep stages, so poor sleep can reduce the benefits of workouts.

steps.heading: How much sleep is enough?
steps.body: Most adults function best with 7–9 hours of sleep per night, according to major sleep health organisations. The quality of sleep matters alongside quantity - fragmented sleep can leave you tired even after 8 hours in bed. Consistent sleep and wake times, a cool and dark room, and avoiding bright screens in the hour before bed are among the most evidence-supported ways to improve sleep quality.

takeaway: Sleep is an underappreciated factor in weight management. Too little sleep raises hunger hormones, suppresses fullness signals, increases cravings for calorie-dense food, and undermines willpower - all at the same time.

sources.title: Brief communication: Sleep curtailment in healthy young men is associated with decreased leptin levels, elevated ghrelin levels, and increased hunger and appetite
sources.note: Landmark study directly demonstrating how sleep restriction raises ghrelin and lowers leptin, increasing hunger.

sources.title: Sleep curtailment is accompanied by increased intake of calories from snacks
sources.note: Controlled study showing sleep-deprived participants consumed more calories, particularly from snacks.
